title: Cracked Tomato: Why It Split and Whether It’s Safe to Eat

seo.title: Can You Eat a Cracked Tomato?
seo.meta_description: Growth cracks are common after rapid water uptake. Dry cracks on a firm tomato can often be trimmed; wet cracks with mold or rot are a reason to toss it.
seo.search_intent: Explain tomato cracking and decide when a split tomato can still be eaten.

excerpt: A dry, healed crack on an otherwise firm tomato is usually a quality issue and can be trimmed. A wet split with mold, slime, off odor, or decaying flesh is a reason to discard the tomato.
content_html:
A cracked tomato is not automatically spoiled. Many cracks form because the fruit expands faster than its skin can stretch, especially after dry conditions are followed by heavy rain or watering. The practical question is whether the crack has dried and healed or is still open, wet, and deteriorating.

A firm tomato with a dry, corky growth crack can often be trimmed and eaten. A deep wet split with slime, mold, leaking tissue, insects, or an off odor is a different situation and should be discarded.

Why tomatoes split

Tomatoes commonly develop radial cracks that run outward from the stem or concentric cracks that circle the shoulders. Penn State Extension links cracking to rapid water uptake, fruit growth, heat, ripening stage, and cultivar susceptibility.

A crack that develops on the plant may dry into a tough, cork-like scar. Once dry, it is mainly a quality defect. A newly opened split offers far less protection against dirt and microorganisms.

Dry and healed is different from wet and open

What the crack looks likePractical decision
Dry, corky, firm tomato, normal smellTrim if desired and use soon
Fresh clean split on a just-picked tomato, no decayWash, trim the damaged area, and use promptly
Deep wet crack or leaking tissueDiscard if deterioration is present
Mold, slime, bad odor, collapsing fleshDiscard
Insects or soil deep in the splitUse a conservative judgment; discard if the damage cannot be cleanly removed

FDA guidance for fresh produce recommends cutting away damaged or bruised areas and discarding produce that looks rotten. That works well for a minor dry crack. It is much less reassuring when the tomato is soft and the split has become a channel into wet decaying tissue.

Use cracked tomatoes sooner

Even a sound cracked tomato has lost part of its protective barrier. Once you decide it is usable, do not make it the tomato you save for next week. It is a good candidate for dinner that day: sauce, soup, salsa that will be eaten promptly, or a cooked dish.

Home canning is a different decision

Do not apply the same rescue logic to shelf-stable home canning. Extension guidance for canning calls for firm, disease-free tomatoes rather than soft, badly cracked, frost-damaged, or decaying fruit. Tested canning recipes are built around predictable ingredients and acidity.

A tomato that is acceptable after trimming for tonight's pasta sauce is not automatically an appropriate canning tomato.

Washing helps, but it does not sterilize a split

Rinsing under running water is part of safe produce preparation. It can remove soil and reduce surface contamination, but it cannot turn a deep, rotten crack into sound tissue. Cut away minor damage; discard decay.

The rule to keep

Dry crack plus firm tomato: usually a use-it-soon problem. Wet crack plus rot, mold, slime, or off odor: a throw-it-out problem. And for home canning, start with intact, high-quality tomatoes.

faq.question: Can you eat a cracked tomato?
faq.answer: Usually, if the crack is dry and the tomato is firm and free of mold or rot. Trim the damaged area and use the tomato promptly.

faq.question: Why do tomatoes crack?
faq.answer: Cracking often occurs when water uptake and fruit expansion happen faster than the skin can stretch, especially after a dry period followed by rain or heavy watering.

faq.question: Can cracked tomatoes be used for home canning?
faq.answer: Home-canning guidance calls for firm, sound tomatoes. Avoid badly cracked, soft, diseased, or decaying fruit for shelf-stable canning.
